title: Why Oil and Water Won't Mix

t: Shake oil and water together as hard as you like. Leave it a minute and it separates again.
Shake oil and water as violently as you can and it mixes for a moment. Stand still and watch it come apart again, on its own, every time.
sub: Nothing pushed them apart. So what did?
No force separated them and nothing was arranged. Work out what did it.

question: Why does oil gather back into a blob?
What drives the oil back together after mixing?
options: The water is what pushes it together
The oil molecules attract each other strongly
The oil is heavier, so it sinks
stages.outcome: The water is what pushes it together
note: Guess before you look — the usual answer is the wrong one.
Commit. The intuitive answer is the second, and it is not correct: the effect is driven from the water's side.

t: The round beads hate water. Bend the string and watch them find each other.
Round beads are oily, square ones are happy in water. Fold the chain until the oily ones are together in the middle.
goal: The oily ones ended up together in the middle. Nobody put them there.
The oily beads gathered inside and the watery ones face out. Nothing arranged that — it is what the water leaves as the likeliest arrangement.

t: A longer chain. Find its best arrangement, and notice the oily ones always end up inside.
Different sequence, same single rule. Find the best arrangement and note that the pattern of the result — buried oil, exposed polar — is invariant even though the shape is not.
goal: Different shape, same idea: the oily bits go inside.
Different geometry, identical principle. This is the same effect that makes a membrane, folds a protein, and splits your salad dressing.

t: Water squeezes the oily bits together. It is called the hydrophobic effect.
This is the hydrophobic effect. The water does the work — oil is pushed together rather than pulling itself together.
The hydrophobic effect is entropic. Water forms an ordered cage around an exposed oily surface; burying that surface frees the caged water, and the entropy gained by the water pays for it.

It is one of the few genuinely counter-intuitive results in undergraduate biochemistry: the association of the nonpolar molecules is not driven by any attraction between them. The driving term sits in the solvent, which is why the effect strengthens with temperature over a wide range instead of weakening.
sub: The oil is not sticky. The water is fussy.
Oil-oil attraction is weak. The water's preference for its own company is what does it.
Which is why the same effect builds a membrane, folds a protein and separates a vinaigrette — one cause, three phenomena.

It is also why soap works: a molecule with an oily tail and a water-loving head can sit at the boundary and satisfy both, which is the whole of detergency and, not coincidentally, the whole of how a cell membrane assembles itself.

q: What actually pushes oil into a blob?
Where does the driving force for hydrophobic association come from?
Why is the hydrophobic effect not an attraction between oily molecules?
options: The water, getting itself out of the way
The oil molecules gripping each other
why: Oily things are not sticky. Water is just much happier next to other water, so it shoves the oil together to get on with it.

The force comes from the solvent. Water has to arrange itself into a rigid cage around an exposed oily surface; shrinking that surface releases the cage, and that release is what drives the association.

The effect is entropic and lives in the water, not enthalpic and living in the oil. The clearest evidence is the temperature dependence: over a broad range hydrophobic association gets stronger as you warm it, which no ordinary attraction between two molecules does.

t: This is why a cell has a wall at all. The oily bits line up and shut the water out.

A membrane is not built by anything. Put molecules with oily tails and water-loving heads into water and they assemble themselves into a double sheet, because that is the arrangement that buries the most oil. Every cell boundary that has ever existed forms for exactly the reason your salad dressing separates.
